## Vision

FCM is the Slack front door to the `everything` monorepo. For the people in the workspace, it is a community bot and an AI assistant that lives where they already talk: it runs the music poll and ad-hoc polls, answers questions with the channel's context, and eventually holds real conversations. For the monorepo's services and agents, it is the one place that holds Slack credentials — they post notifications, ask a human a question, or receive a slash command through FCM instead of each one integrating with Slack. All of this runs on free tiers: FCM uses Slack's free Bolt/Socket Mode surface, never Slack's paid agent platform. Agent reasoning lives in whagent_net, not in FCM.

## Personas

- **Community member** — a person in the Slack workspace who uses the social and AI features (`/wai`, the music poll, `/wpoll`, and later AI conversations and game-server status).
- **Service / agent** — another monorepo system (manmanv2, whagent_net, deploy tooling, krill agents) that uses FCM to reach people in Slack.
- **Operator** — runs the FCM deployment. This is the same person who owns the workspace and needs it to be deployable and debuggable.

## Load-bearing decisions

### LB1 — Services reach Slack through one FCM-owned message contract

At risk: C6, C7 (`Next`, M2), C10, C11 (`Later`).
  Decide now: FCM is the only system that holds Slack tokens. When M2 opens the
  service-to-Slack path, it is a single FCM-owned, versioned JSON contract on
  RabbitMQ, defined in one place, where new fields are added and existing ones are
  never changed. It is not one bespoke subscriber per producer, which is what the
  V1 `bot/subscribe` service is. The first version of the contract has three
  parts, even though M2 uses only the first two: a logical `route` name that FCM
  resolves through its `slackspecialchannel` tables, so producers never hold
  Slack channel IDs; a producer-scoped message key, so a repeat event edits the
  same Slack message instead of posting a new one (the generic form of
  `manmanstatusupdate.slack_message_id`); and an optional correlation ID and
  reply route, so a human's answer or a routed slash command comes back on the
  same contract. Translating a domain's events into Slack messages is the job of
  an adapter that emits this contract — FCM takes no compile-time dependency on
  another domain's generated clients, which is why FCM's build breaks today when
  manman V1 changes. M1's V1 removal therefore keeps the `slackspecialchannel`
  tables and drops only the `manman_dev` usage: those tables become the route
  table. C14, the legacy V1 subscribe path, is what this replaces.
  Stays cheap: Block Kit rendering, which producers exist, whether the manmanv2
  adapter runs in FCM's deployment or next to manmanv2, rate limiting, how an
  operator maps routes to channels, and C11's command registry. What is
  expensive later: once several services publish raw channel IDs in
  fire-and-forget payloads, adding edit-in-place or replies means changing every
  producer at the same time.
  Capability numbers in this body are krill display numbers, which are assigned
  per product in creation order and so do not match the C-numbers in the
  pre-onboarding hand-authored brief. See the mapping note on this Product.

### LB2 — FCM holds no agent state; whagent_net owns conversations

At risk: C8, C12.
  Decide now: no milestone adds multi-turn transcript history, tool calling, or
  agent definitions to FCM. FCM's only conversation state is a mapping from a
  Slack thread (`channel` plus `thread_ts`) to a whagent_net session ID, plus
  the per-channel agent binding that selects which agent serves a channel.
  Transcripts, turns, caps, and tools stay in whagent_net (its LB1 and LB5).
  FCM relays thread replies by polling `GetSession` and `ReadTranscript` on a
  short interval from inside its Temporal workflow rather than subscribing to
  whagent_net's session event exchange; that poll is a transport detail, not
  FCM holding a second copy of the conversation. `genaitext` stays an audit
  log, not conversation memory.
  Stays cheap: replacing the poll with an event exchange once whagent_net grows
  one, the `/wai` prompt chain, the Gemini SDK and model upgrade, whether
  `/wai` is later re-implemented as a whagent agent, and how thread replies are
  rendered. What is expensive later: a second conversation store in FCM would
  have to be migrated into whagent_net's transcript record or reconciled with
  it, and in the meantime Slack users would see two assistants with different
  memories.
  This supersedes the original LB2, which forbade polling outright; the
  commitment that mattered — FCM holds no conversation state of its own — is
  unchanged, and the transport is now named as the code actually implements
  it. Note that C8 is substantially built already; see the scope-note on it.
  Capability numbers here are krill display numbers, not the pre-onboarding
  brief's. See the mapping note on this Product.

### LB3 — The Slack user is the downstream principal, never FCM's service account

At risk: C8, C9, C10, C12.
  Decide now: when FCM acts in another system for a person, it authenticates as
  its own service account and names that person as the on-behalf-of subject
  using whagent_net's `(iss, sub, kind)` shape (its LB2). The asserted subject
  is the person's **linked Keycloak identity** — Keycloak's `iss` and `sub`,
  with `kind` human — not the raw Slack team and user IDs. Slack's team and user
  IDs are the lookup key that resolves a Slack account to its Keycloak link,
  never the asserted subject. FCM therefore never starts a whagent session or a
  manmanv2 action under its own identity for a request a human triggered, and
  never asserts a Slack-native subject a downstream system would have to
  special-case. The user sync (C3) already records each user's team, and M1
  must keep doing so.
  Stays cheap: linking Slack users to Keycloak accounts, the mint-and-callback
  flow that creates those links, each system's authorization policy (for
  example, who may restart a server), and display names. What is expensive
  later: sessions and actions recorded under FCM's own identity — or under a
  Slack-native subject a downstream system cannot resolve — can never be
  re-attributed to the person who asked, so every "who did this" rollup and
  every per-person permission would have to start with no history. A user with
  no completed identity link gets no `on_behalf_of` at all, which is why C13,
  the identity-link web app, is a user-facing capability in its own right.
  This supersedes the original LB3, which named the Slack team ID and Slack user
  ID as `iss` and `sub`; the commitment that mattered — the human is the
  principal, never FCM's service account — is unchanged, and the subject is now
  named as the code actually asserts it. Capability numbers here are krill
  display numbers, not the pre-onboarding brief's; see the mapping note on this
  Product.

## Non-goals

**Permanent:**

- **manman V1 support.** FCM will not integrate with or maintain compatibility with the legacy manman V1 system. Game-server features target manmanv2 only.
- **Slack's paid AI/agent platform.** FCM uses the free Bolt/Socket Mode API. It does not use Slack-hosted agents, Slack AI, or any feature that needs a paid Slack plan.
